newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia data shows low inflation, growing economy.
newsitem.headline: Australia data shows low inflation, growing economy.

text.p: Australia's economy is emerging from a sluggish 1996 on a positive note, with economists saying early economic indicators for 1997 point to a period of strong growth and low inflation.
The latest two pieces of information, released on Thursday, showed wages pressures were in check and continued optimism about investment was a key driver of growth.
Despite a fall in private new capital expenditure of 2.4 percent in December, against median expectations of a 2.1 percent rise, businesses remain optimistic on the capital expenditure outlook.

"There is a very strong momentum in capital expenditure expectations, which is very important going forward, and it validates the sort of view the Reserve Bank was expressing, that there is still quite a strong recovery underway," Deutsche Morgan Grenfell senior economist Bruce Hockman said.
The December weakness was due to the deferral of some large construction projects in the mining and transport industries, and delays to other projects, the statistics bureau said.
The capex report also included a survey of expected investment. The forecast for the 1996/97 (July/June) fiscal year was 1.5 percent higher than the September quarter estimate.
The figure also included businesses' first estimate of spending in 1997/98. At 10.1 percent higher than the same estimate for 1996/97, analysts said it was a bullish sign for investment.
"The forward looking capex measures, including the first look at 1997/98, remain robust," Bankers Trust Australia chief economist Chris Caton said.
However, he added capex may not be as strong in the second half of 1996/97 as earlier thought, a sentiment others shared.
While capex growth was still going to be strong in 1996/97, analysts said the government's revised forecast of a 17 percent rise, announced last month, may now be slightly optimistic.
"The original forecast of 14 percent capex growth from last August's budget seems a better bet," said Nomura Research senior economist Andrew Pease, but added the outlook was positive.

Also released on Thursday was final wages data for the three months to November 1996. The numbers confirmed preliminary data from earlier in the month that average weekly ordinary time earnings rose 1.2 percent in the quarter, to be up 3.9 percent in the year.
Of most interest to economists in the final figures was the pace of wages growth in the private sector.
They rose 0.8 percent in the quarter to be up 2.8 percent over the year, down from 3.5 percent in the year to August.
"I like the private sector outcome," Dresdner Australia chief economist Rob Henderson said.
"Coming on top of the figures we got yesterday on enterprise bargaining, I think the inflation outlook is excellent."

Citibank Australia economists said that together with other data suggesting a strengthening, low inflation economy, "the booming business investment numbers must have the policy makers at the RBA and those in Treasury ready to celebrate the near- utopian fundamentals".
"The only parts of the equation missing are the persistently high level of unemployment and the problem of the net income deficit," they said in a commentary.

Given signs of stronger activity and some uncertainties over wages in 1997, including the outcome of the union movement's "living wage" claim, the RBA was seen leaving interest rates steady despite the positive inflation outlook.
"Cash rates look set to stay on hold at 6.0 percent for some time to come," UBS Australia chief economist Steve Roberts said.
